title: Watch (Mark 13)
hook: the Temple will fall, no one knows the hour, so watch

segments.voice: Yesterday, the widow's two mites: she gave more than all the rich, because she gave all she had. Your line was all she had. What small thing did it cost you? Today they leave the Temple, and the week ends with one word. Day two hundred twenty-four.

Picture a small-town fisherman seeing a great city for the first time. As they walk out of the Temple, one of the disciples can't help himself: Master, look at these stones! Look at these buildings! And they were enormous, some of the biggest cut stones in the ancient world, gleaming on the hill. Jesus looks at them and says every stone will be thrown down. Then he climbs the Mount of Olives, sits facing the Temple, and four of the disciples ask him quietly: when? What happens next is the longest speech Jesus gives in all of Mark.
screen: `LOOK AT THESE STONES!` → `EVERY STONE THROWN DOWN.` → `WHEN? THE LONGEST SPEECH IN MARK.`

segments.voice: First, the stones. In the Douay-Rheims: "There shall not be left a stone upon a stone, that shall not be thrown down." About forty years later, in the year 70, Roman armies crushed a revolt and burned the Temple. For Mark's first readers, this may have been very recent news. Second, the troubles. Jesus speaks of wars and rumors of wars, earthquakes, famines, false messiahs, families divided, persecution. It's hard to hear. But he keeps saying: don't be alarmed. The end is not yet. Hold on. Third, the surprise. After all those signs, he says something almost no one expects: "But of that day or hour no man knoweth, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father." Nobody gets a date. Not the angels. Not even the Son. Christians have argued for centuries about what it means that the Son doesn't know; the Church has read it in light of his true humanity, and of what was his to reveal. What's certain is this: anyone who sets a date for the end of the world is going against this verse. Fourth, the doorkeeper. Jesus ends with a picture: a man goes on a journey and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake, because the master might come back in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. Some readers notice those four times come back in the next chapters: the supper in the evening, the garden at night, Peter at cockcrow, Pilate in the morning. And the last line of the speech: "And what I say to you, I say to all: Watch." This week in Mark: the children, the rich man, Bartimaeus, the fig tree, Caesar's coin, the widow. And now, one word for everyone.
screen: `NOT A STONE UPON A STONE.` · `THE END IS NOT YET.` · `NO ONE KNOWS THE DAY OR HOUR.` · `THE DOORKEEPER STAYS AWAKE.` · then, large: `WHAT I SAY TO YOU, I SAY TO ALL: WATCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish today as if it matters. Settle and breathe. Watching doesn't mean staring at the sky or reading the news in a panic. It means being awake to what's in front of you. Think through the rest of today. One unfinished thing you've been putting off. One person you haven't really paid attention to. Choose one, and decide to finish it, or face them, before you sleep. If you pray, you can offer the rest of the day. The bell holds the time.
Watch. The last word of Jesus's longest speech in Mark: stay awake, because no one knows the hour. Today's word.
Your line: watch. Today, three times, stop and ask: am I awake right now, or on autopilot? Then do the next thing awake. Day two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Jesus's call to watch at the start of Advent each year, and profess in the Creed that Christ will come again, while the Church teaches that no one can know the day or the hour.

original.note: Greek: stay awake, keep watch. the name Gregory comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scary chapter about the end of the world.
what it means: troubles will come, no one knows the hour, so stay awake to what's in front of you.
what a scholar hears: grēgoreite, keep awake; four night watches (evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning) that some readers map onto the passion.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 13:2, 13:32 and 13:37 given from memory; confirm.

The Son's not knowing (13:32): the script says only that the Church reads it 'in light of his true humanity, and of what was his to reveal' (cf. CCC 474). A Keeper should confirm this summary is adequate.
Dating of Mark relative to AD 70 is debated; the script says the news 'may have been very recent'. Confirm.
The mapping of the four watches onto the passion (14:17, 14:41?, 14:72, 15:1) is a known reading (e.g. R. H. Lightfoot); presented as 'some readers notice'. Confirm.
